extracted.intended_audience: medical practitioners, public-health officials, and scientifically literate general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards concerning vaccination practice (preservation and transmission of vaccine virus), experimental approaches to disease-germs (including animal experiments and replication), and principles of sound scientific inquiry and public-health response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain original vaccinia stock by heifer transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: The Government should maintain an establishment on a sufficient scale so every vaccination and revaccination may be performed with lymph derived from the original cow-stock, without any humanization whatever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuous transmission of vaccinia through a succession of heifers preserves its original efficacy and potency, excludes human contamination, and prevents impairment of protective influence by prolonged 'cultivation' in humans. Dr. Martin and the Bougival/heifer-stock examples are cited as practical confirmations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'humanization' of vaccine virus
rubrics_metrics.description: Vaccinia tends to degenerate — i.e., to lose its protective power — in proportion to the remoteness of its derivation from the original (cow) stock; 'humanized' vaccinia shows diminished potency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clinical observations (smaller vesicles, faster course, less constitutional disturbance) and Dr. Martin's experiments (retro-vaccination failing beyond the third remove from human into bovine) support that many alleged vaccine 'failures' are attributable to degeneration by human transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer genuine heifer-lymph (including dried on ivory 'points') following expert methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Vaccination from heifer-stock (properly practiced) is as successful as vaccination from the human arm and produces the true old Jennerian vesicle without deterioration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dr. Martin's method (including use of Bougival heifer-stock and dried lymph on ivory points) is reported to match or exceed human lymph in proportion of 'takes' and to avoid some 'accidents' seen with direct cow-stock vaccination, provided practitioners follow his practiced instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict enforcement and immediate vaccination/revaccination during outbreaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Municipal authorities should insist on immediate vaccination and revaccination of all dwellers in infected localities to control and prevent recurrence of outbreaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience in the United States during severe small-pox outbreaks showed that local municipal compulsion of vaccination/revaccination, backed by authority, was effective in controlling epidemics even where no general registration system existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: When replicating experimental successes, carefully imitate original conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Failures of replication are not necessarily contradictory of reported successes; careful imitation of the conditions under which successes were obtained is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The negative results of some experimenters (e.g., Chauveau, Belgian Commission, Burdon-Sanderson's contemporaries) should prompt investigators to reproduce the precise methods and conditions of the original successful experiments (consulting the original practitioners when possible) and to undertake thorough, precautioned testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experiments on living animals where necessary to advance knowledge of disease
rubrics_metrics.description: Important contributions to the knowledge of disease, and of its cure and prevention, come from experiments performed on living animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that many promising advances (Pasteurian lines, tubercle microphyte work, etc.) inherently depend on animal experiments and that such experimental work is often the only route to crucial discoveries about pathogenesis and prevention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt Pasteurian approach cautiously and reinvestigate unsettled fundamental questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume identity of vaccinia and variola or other fundamental biological equivalences without further research under new methods; treat Pasteur's terminology as a compliment rather than proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pasteur himself did not consider the identity of vaccinia and variola decided; investigators (and policy-makers) should support thorough reinvestigations, taking advantage of the new light from Pastorian methods while avoiding premature conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply statistical methods as a primary basis for sound conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistics are 'the anatomy and physiology of the social body' and should be used extensively in research to avoid impressions and partial judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broca advocates applying means and statistical analysis across observations and populations (including anatomy and anthropology) so that conclusions rest on broad data rather than isolated impressions — check facts across regions and practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broca's principles of scientific inquiry and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific work should submit received doctrines to independent criticism, check classical descriptions against positive observations, appeal to experience from many sources, follow ideas from origin to development, and seek reality even when authority may suffer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers and scientific writers should combine criticism and observation, unite clinics and history, 'profiting by ancient and modern facts, checking one with another, despising none,' and 'consecrate the rights of the true inventors.' This is offered as a model 'confession of faith' for scientific writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Found and maintain scientific societies with free scope but exclusive scientific character
rubrics_metrics.description: New scientific societies should ensure free scope for questions relating to mankind while maintaining an exclusively scientific character to dispel political or social suspicions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broca's experience founding the Anthropological Society shows the need to balance openness of inquiry with explicit scientific purpose and careful administration (including responsible leadership and transparent publication) to gain recognition and avoid censorship or suspicion.
